learn.intro: How far was Britain's Industrial Revolution built on the world beyond Britain? And how revolutionary was the Agricultural Revolution that came before it? This topic follows cotton from enslaved labour in the Americas to Lancashire's mills, then returns to the English countryside.

sections.title: 1. The revolution behind the revolution

blocks.p: A chain connected Britain's industry to the wider world:

ul: Enslaved Africans were forced to grow raw cotton on plantations in the Americas.
Cotton was shipped through British ports such as Liverpool, Bristol and Glasgow, which grew rich on Atlantic trade.
It was processed into cloth in Lancashire's mills.
Finished cloth was sold in Britain, Europe and colonial and global markets, generating profits that could be reinvested.

blocks.p: Profits linked to the slave trade and colonial trade also fed banking, insurance and infrastructure in port cities.

This is a genuine debate. The historian Eric Williams argued in "Capitalism and Slavery" (1944) that profits from slavery were a crucial engine of British industrial capital. Other historians argue those profits were too small a share of total investment to be the main cause. The most defensible position is that global and domestic factors were interconnected: mills needed slave-grown cotton AND British capital, coal, machines and workers.

evidence: Liverpool, Bristol and Glasgow grew rich on Atlantic trade.

blocks.p: Before enclosure, much land was farmed in open strips shared by a village, with common land for grazing and fuel. Enclosure fenced it into larger private fields. Enclosure Acts were especially numerous from the 1760s to the 1830s.

ul: Jethro Tull's seed drill (1701) sowed seed in straight rows, using seed more efficiently than scattering by hand.
Viscount "Turnip" Townshend popularised four-field crop rotation (wheat, turnips, barley, clover), keeping soil fertile without leaving fields fallow, and providing winter animal feed.
Robert Bakewell's selective breeding produced larger, faster-maturing sheep and cattle.

blocks.p: Food production rose, supporting a growing population and freeing workers for industry. But enclosure caused real hardship: smallholders and labourers lost rights to common land, pushing some into poverty, wage labour or migration to towns. A landowner and a labourer might disagree about whether this was a "revolution", or progress.

timeline.event: Robert Bakewell develops selective breeding; Enclosure Acts multiply.
Slavery is abolished in most of the British Empire.

misconceptions.wrong: Slavery caused the Industrial Revolution on its own.
misconceptions.right: It was significant but interconnected with domestic factors. Historians debate how much it mattered.

misconceptions.wrong: Slavery had nothing to do with industrialisation.
misconceptions.right: Slave-grown cotton fed Lancashire's mills and Atlantic trade profits flowed into British ports.
It raised output but took common rights from many villagers.

sources.title: "Capitalism and Slavery" by Eric Williams
sources.origin: Written by a Trinidadian historian, based on his Oxford doctoral research.
sources.purpose: To argue that slavery's profits helped fund British industrialisation, and that economics shaped abolition.
sources.usefulness: A landmark interpretation that started the debate. Later historians have challenged parts of the economic argument.

evidence.q: Explain the chain connecting enslaved labour to Lancashire's mills.
evidence.model: Enslaved Africans were forced to grow raw cotton on plantations in the Americas; it was shipped through ports such as Liverpool to Lancashire's mills, where it was spun and woven into cloth for sale.

evidence.q: Give evidence that enclosure was both progress and hardship.
evidence.model: Enclosure made new methods like crop rotation easier, increasing food production, but smallholders lost rights to common land, pushing some into poverty or migration.

sources.label: Source A
sources.provenance: From "Capitalism and Slavery" (1944) by the Trinidadian historian Eric Williams, based on his doctoral research at Oxford.
sources.text: Williams argues that the profits of the slave trade and of plantations in the Caribbean helped provide money for British banks, shipping and industry, and that ports such as Liverpool and Bristol grew rich on Atlantic trade. He also argues that Britain abolished the slave trade partly because it had become less profitable.

questions.sources_note: Source A is described in our own words for revision practice. In the exam you will be given the source itself.
